faq.a: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; ampicillin penetrates CSF and is effective against this organism.
faq.q: Why is ampicillin the drug of choice for Listeria?

faq.a: No, steroids are contraindicated as they may worsen outcomes in Listeria infections.
faq.q: Can steroids be used in Listeria meningitis?

faq.q: What is the typical CSF profile in Listeria meningitis?

exam: A 3‑day‑old infant presents with fever and poor feeding. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose. What is the most likely organism and first‑line treatment? — Listeria monocytogenes; start ampicillin plus gentamicin.

A 5‑year‑old child with HIV presents with headache and neck stiffness. CSF culture is negative after 48 hours of antibiotics. What is the next step? — Repeat CSF culture and consider Listeria; add ampicillin.
Why are cephalosporins ineffective against Listeria? — Listeria has low affinity for cephalosporin binding sites; it is intrinsically resistant.
A neonate develops seizures after starting empiric ceftriaxone for suspected meningitis. What should be added? — Ampicillin, because Listeria is a common cause in neonates.
What laboratory finding would most strongly suggest Listeria over other bacterial meningitis? — Normal CSF glucose with lymphocytic pleocytosis.
In a low‑resource setting, CSF culture is unavailable. Which diagnostic test can rapidly confirm Listeria? — CSF PCR for Listeria.
ai.title: Listeria Meningitis in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram‑positive rod that can cause meningitis, especially in neonates, the elderly and immunocompromised. Early recognition and prompt ampicillin‑based therapy are essential.

b: Gram‑positive rod, catalase positive, beta‑hemolytic on blood agar
sections.p: Listeria meningitis is a bacterial meningitis caused by L. monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular organism. Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF culture or PCR, with typical CSF showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and mildly raised protein.

t.b: Detects gram‑positive rods; a positive result strongly suggests Listeria
Growth of beta‑hemolytic colonies confirms diagnosis
Rapid detection when culture is negative or delayed

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Glasgow Coma Scale and presence of seizures or focal deficits. Early onset (within 7 days of birth) is more fulminant.

b: Neonatal exposure to contaminated dairy or unpasteurised food
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, common predisposing factors include neonatal exposure to contaminated food, maternal HIV, and malnutrition.
Neonates present with irritability, poor feeding, fever, and sometimes seizures. Older children may have headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and altered consciousness.
Basic investigations are often limited; focus on CSF analysis and basic labs.

t.b: Look for neutrophilia; normal or mild leukocytosis may be seen
Elevated in bacterial meningitis; helps differentiate from viral
May grow Listeria in neonates; guides antibiotic choice
Rule out abscess or hydrocephalus; useful if focal deficits

sections.p: Rapid deterioration, seizures, focal neurological signs, and hydrocephalus are urgent red flags.

b: Avoid steroids unless bacterial meningitis is confirmed to be non‑Listeria
sections.p: Empiric therapy should include ampicillin plus gentamicin; adjust once culture results are available. Supportive care and monitoring of intracranial pressure are essential.
Repeat CSF culture until sterile. Preventive measures include maternal screening for Listeria, safe food handling, and early treatment of neonatal sepsis.
Neonatal meningitis due to Group B Streptococcus or E. coli; viral meningitis; tuberculous meningitis.
CSF glucose may be normal in Listeria, unlike other bacterial meningitis; cultures can be negative if antibiotics were given early.
